evidence: createApp() acts as the composition root: it creates InMemoryUserRepository, InMemoryProjectRepository, InMemoryTaskRepository, UuidGenerator, UserService and TaskManagementService (infrastructure wiring).

Route handlers such as app.post('/projects/:projectId/tasks') and app.get('/projects/:projectId/tasks') only read req.params, req.body and req.query, then call service methods and return res.json (transport).
The error middleware maps ValidationError to 400, NotFoundError to 404, ConflictError to 409 and SyntaxError to 400 (HTTP adapter work).
The PUT /tasks/:taskId/assignee handler checks that assigneeId is present and is a string. This is request-shape validation at the transport boundary, not a business rule.
Business operations (markDone, assignTask, listTasks filtering) are left to TaskManagementService in the application layer.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: src/infrastructure/app.ts belongs to the infrastructure layer, and everything it does fits that layer. It wires up dependencies (in-memory repositories, the ID generator and the application services) and defines the Express routes. Those routes read request parameters and bodies, pass the work to application services, and send back HTTP responses. It also maps domain errors to HTTP status codes in the error middleware. All of this is transport and framework work. The only check that looks like a rule is in the PUT /tasks/:taskId/assignee handler, which confirms assigneeId is a non-empty string. That is checking the shape of the request at the transport boundary, not a domain rule. Task status changes, assignment rules and filtering are all handled by TaskManagementService. The small str() helper only coerces query-string values to strings, which is also transport work.
